wokeTrap.explanation: Madame Web is not a woke trap. The film's girl-power framing is visible from the first trailer. Anyone who sees the marketing, three young women destined to become Spider-Women under the protection of a reluctant female mentor, knows exactly what they are getting. The woke content, such as it is, is mild and mostly inept. There is no ideological bait-and-switch. The bigger deception is the trailer itself, which implies a competently made superhero film. That is the real trap.

woke_trap_assessment.explanation: NOT A WOKE TRAP. The all-female hero ensemble, the maternal protection arc, and the girl-boss framing are all visible from marketing materials and the first ten minutes. There is nothing hidden. Conservative viewers will recognize the ideological territory immediately. The real surprise is not the ideology but the staggering incompetence of the filmmaking. This is a film that fails on craft before it fails on politics.

director.name: S.J. Clarkson
director.ideology: MODERATE/PROGRESSIVE. Clarkson is a veteran TV director whose credits lean toward prestige television. Her feature film debut here is a catastrophic misfire, but her prior work on Jessica Jones, The Defenders, Succession, and Anatomy of a Scandal suggests a filmmaker comfortable working within both progressive and institutional frameworks without strong personal ideological branding.
director.profile: S.J. Clarkson is a British director born in 1974 who built her career entirely in television before Madame Web became her feature debut. Her credits are impressive in breadth: Jessica Jones, The Defenders, Succession, Anatomy of a Scandal, Collateral, Orange Is the New Black, Dexter, House, Heroes, Life on Mars, and Vinyl. She co-created the British series Mistresses in 2008. Clarkson was hired by Sony in May 2020 to develop and direct their first female-centric Marvel film. She also co-wrote the screenplay alongside Claire Parker, Matt Sazama, and Burk Sharpless. Her Jessica Jones work is the most relevant predecessor here: she directed episodes of a show about a reluctant, abrasive female superhero with psychological damage, which is essentially the template she tried to apply to Cassie Webb. The difference is that Jessica Jones had sharp writing, a compelling villain in Kilgrave, and a star in Krysten Ritter who sold the damaged-hero routine with conviction. Madame Web has none of these things. Clarkson described Cassie as a loner on the outer edges, quirky and abrasive, and compared her to Jessica Jones. The comparison only highlights how far short this film falls.

writer.name: Matt Sazama & Burk Sharpless, Claire Parker, S.J. Clarkson
writer.profile: The screenplay carries four credited writers, which is rarely a good sign. Matt Sazama and Burk Sharpless are the most notable names, and their track record is a graveyard of studio tentpoles: Dracula Untold (2014), The Last Witch Hunter (2015), Gods of Egypt (2016), Power Rangers (2017), and Morbius (2022). Every single one of these films was either a critical failure, a box office bomb, or both. Their involvement with Madame Web should have been the first red flag. Claire Parker has no other screenwriting credits. S.J. Clarkson's involvement as co-writer was only revealed in November 2023, months before release, suggesting either late rewrites or a desire to distance herself from the original draft. The script is the film's most catastrophic failure: the dialogue is stilted, the plot is driven entirely by convenience and contrivance, characters lack dimension, and the narrative logic collapses under the slightest scrutiny. Kerem Sanga (The Big Sick) wrote an earlier story draft.

lead_producer.name: Lorenzo di Bonaventura
lead_producer.company: Columbia Pictures / Marvel Entertainment / Di Bonaventura Pictures

composer.name: Johan Soderqvist
composer.profile: Swedish composer known for scoring Let the Right One In (2008) and Kon-Tiki (2012). A frequent collaborator of Clarkson's from her TV work. His score for Madame Web is the film's least offensive element: competent, atmospheric, and occasionally effective at building tension that the script and direction cannot sustain.

top_performers.name: Adam Scott
top_performers.note: Scott brings natural warmth and charm to his limited screen time as Ben Parker. He is the only performer in the film who seems to understand what movie he is in and calibrates his energy accordingly. His chemistry with Johnson works, and his scenes provide the film's only moments of genuine human connection. He deserved more screen time.

top_performers.name: Isabela Merced
top_performers.note: Merced does her best with a thinly written role. Her character Anya Corazon has the most potentially interesting backstory, a teenage girl fending for herself after her father's deportation, and Merced brings enough natural intelligence and presence to make you wish the script had given her something real to work with.

bottom_performers.name: Dakota Johnson
bottom_performers.note: Johnson's lead performance is the film's most discussed failure. She appears to be operating in a state of permanent detachment, delivering lines as though she is reading them for the first time from a teleprompter in another room. Her two emotional registers are bored and slightly less bored. In scenes where her character should be panicking, grieving, or fighting for survival, Johnson projects the energy of someone who misplaced her phone. The Razzie for Worst Actress was earned.

bottom_performers.name: Tahar Rahim
bottom_performers.note: Rahim is a genuinely talented actor (A Prophet, The Mauritanian) who is completely destroyed by this film. His villain Ezekiel Sims is undermined at every level: the writing gives him nothing beyond 'kill the teenagers,' the costume is a generic Spider-Man knockoff, and most damningly, his dialogue appears to have been heavily re-dubbed in post-production via ADR. His lip movements frequently do not match the audio. The result is a villain who sounds like he is being voiced by someone in a recording booth a continent away. Reports suggest the studio changed his dialogue after filming, resulting in the audio-visual disconnect that became one of the film's most mocked elements.

fidelityCasting.sourceTitle: Madame Web (first appearance: The Amazing Spider-Man #210, 1980, created by Denny O'Neil and John Romita Jr.)
fidelityCasting.assessment: The adaptation takes enormous liberties with the source material. In the comics, Cassandra Webb is an elderly, blind, paralyzed woman connected to a life-support system that resembles a spider web. She is a fully developed clairvoyant who serves as a mentor figure to Spider-Man. The film reimagines her as a thirty-something paramedic in the process of discovering her powers, essentially making her a completely different character who shares only a name and the vague concept of clairvoyance with the comic version. The three Spider-Women, Julia Cornwall, Anya Corazon, and Mattie Franklin, are drawn from various Spider-Man comics but are depicted here as powerless teenagers rather than established heroes. We only see them in their Spider-Women costumes in brief flash-forward visions, making the entire film essentially a prologue to the story audiences actually wanted to see. Ezekiel Sims is radically reimagined from the comics, where he was a complex anti-hero connected to mystical spider-totems. Here, he is flattened into a generic villain in a black-and-red Spider-Man suit who wants to murder teenagers. Adam Scott plays Ben Parker (Uncle Ben) as a young paramedic, and Emma Roberts appears as Mary Parker, whose newborn son is obviously Peter Parker. The Spider-Man connections are shameless, especially since Sony cannot actually use Spider-Man in these films, so they function as references to a better franchise the audience would rather be watching.

celebrityMentions.name: Dakota Johnson
celebrityMentions.context: Lead actress. Became a reluctant meme generator during the film's promotional tour, where her visibly unenthusiastic interviews went viral. Her candid admission that she was drawn to the project because of its 'connection to nature and healing' became a source of mockery. Won the Razzie for Worst Actress. Johnson is best known for the Fifty Shades franchise and is the daughter of actors Don Johnson and Melanie Griffith.

celebrityMentions.name: Sydney Sweeney
celebrityMentions.context: Plays Julia Cornwall. Sweeney was one of television's hottest stars at the time of filming, riding the success of Euphoria and The White Lotus. Her involvement was the film's biggest marketing asset, but the role gives her almost nothing to do. She spends most of the film running, hiding, or looking concerned. The film's failure did not damage her career, as she had already established enough credibility elsewhere.

celebrityMentions.name: Tahar Rahim
celebrityMentions.context: Plays the villain Ezekiel Sims. A critically acclaimed French actor known for A Prophet (2009) and The Mauritanian (2021). His performance was sabotaged by extensive ADR re-dubbing that made his dialogue consistently out of sync with his lip movements, turning what could have been a serviceable villain into an unintentional comedy element.

celebrityMentions.name: Adam Scott
celebrityMentions.context: Plays Ben Parker (Uncle Ben). A fan-favorite actor from Parks and Recreation, Severance, and Party Down. His warm, natural performance stands out as the film's single bright spot. His presence also serves as the film's most naked Spider-Man connection: this is Peter Parker's uncle as a young man.

contentWarnings: Standard superhero action violence throughout, including fights, chases, and explosions
A pregnant woman is shot and killed in the opening sequence (set in 1973)
The villain murders multiple people on screen, including choking and using a neurotoxin
Three teenage girls are repeatedly stalked and hunted by an adult man who wants to murder them
A character dies after falling into water during an emergency rescue
Brief references to immigration enforcement and deportation as backstory for one character
A woman is seduced and killed by the villain in one scene
No sexual content beyond brief romantic tension
parentalGuidance.guidance: Despite its PG-13 rating, Madame Web is largely tame by superhero standards. The violence is mostly bloodless. The scariest element for younger viewers may be the premise itself: three teenage girls being relentlessly hunted by a superpowered adult man who wants to kill them. The opening sequence, where a pregnant woman is betrayed and shot by a colleague in the Amazon rainforest, is the film's most intense scene and may upset sensitive children. Otherwise, this is standard superhero fare with no sexual content, strong language, or substance use. The film's biggest danger to children is boredom.

summary.overall:
Madame Web is one of the most comprehensively terrible superhero films ever produced by a major studio. It earned an 11% on Rotten Tomatoes, grossed $100.5 million worldwide against a budget of $80-100 million (a catastrophic loss after marketing costs), and won three Golden Raspberry Awards: Worst Picture, Worst Actress, and Worst Screenplay. These accolades are all deserved.

The premise is this: Cassandra Webb (Dakota Johnson) is a New York City paramedic who, after a near-death experience, begins having visions of the future. She discovers that a villain named Ezekiel Sims (Tahar Rahim) is hunting three teenage girls, Julia Cornwall (Sydney Sweeney), Anya Corazon (Isabela Merced), and Mattie Franklin (Celeste O'Connor), because he has foreseen that they will become Spider-Women and kill him. Cassie must protect the girls, confront the truth about her mother's death in the Amazon, and learn to control her clairvoyant powers.

On paper, this is workable. A reluctant mentor with psychic abilities protecting three future heroes from a precognitive villain is a perfectly fine structure for a superhero origin story. The problem is execution. Every single element fails.

The script, credited to four writers including the team responsible for Morbius, is a disaster of convenience and contrivance. Characters make decisions that no rational person would ever make because the plot requires them to. Cassie is wanted for kidnapping and possibly murder, yet she walks freely through New York City, boards an international flight to Peru, and moves around without taking basic precautions to hide her identity. She arrives in the Peruvian Amazon and immediately finds the exact person she is looking for. A wonder bar appears beneath a parked car at the precise moment she needs it. The three teenagers are told to stay put and promptly leave to go to a diner, where the villain naturally finds them. This happens not once but repeatedly. The film's plot runs entirely on characters being stupid enough to create danger.

Dakota Johnson's lead performance has become legendary for the wrong reasons. She delivers every line with the emotional investment of someone waiting for a delayed flight. In scenes requiring fear, urgency, or grief, she barely registers a pulse. There are moments when people die in front of her and her reaction suggests mild annoyance rather than horror. Whether this is a performance choice (playing Cassie as emotionally numb), a direction failure (Clarkson not getting the range she needed), or simply disinterest (Johnson visibly did not want to be here), the result is a protagonist you cannot care about because she does not appear to care about anything herself.

Tahar Rahim's villain fares even worse, though through less fault of his own. Rahim is a genuinely talented actor. His performance in A Prophet is electrifying. Here, the studio apparently changed significant amounts of his dialogue in post-production, resulting in ADR dubbing that frequently does not match his lip movements. The effect is disorienting and unintentionally hilarious. He looks like a foreign film that has been badly dubbed into English, except this is supposed to be the final product. His motivation (kill teenagers before they kill him) is paper-thin, and his powers (vague spider abilities plus a black-and-red suit) make him a discount Spider-Man fighting a discount psychic.

The three young actresses are wasted. Sweeney, Merced, and O'Connor have varying degrees of talent, but the script gives them nothing to play except victims who need saving. We see them in their Spider-Women costumes only in brief flash-forward visions. The entire film is essentially a prologue to the story you want to see, and that story never arrives. Sony cannot actually use Spider-Man in these films, so the Spider-Women tease is all tease and no payoff.

The ideological content is mild and mostly botched. The film clearly wants to be a female empowerment story: a woman discovers her power, mentors three young women, and defeats a male villain through cunning rather than brute force. But the execution is so limp that the empowerment message never lands. Cassie does not feel empowered. She feels confused and annoyed for two hours and then the movie ends. The three girls do not grow into heroes. They remain passive throughout.

There are specific woke markers. Anya Corazon's backstory involves her father being deported, leaving her alone. One character wears a shirt with a slogan about girls and math. A baby shower scene contrasts Cassie's abrasive independence against traditionally feminine women who are written as shallow. But none of it coheres into an ideological project because the filmmakers were too incompetent to execute one. The wokeness is there in the ingredients but the recipe is burned beyond recognition.

The traditional elements, what few exist, are genuine. The maternal thread is the film's strongest asset. Cassie's mother died trying to save her from a congenital illness. Cassie's arc is about accepting the same responsibility: she becomes the protector of three vulnerable girls because that is what her mother would have done. The self-sacrifice theme is real. Cassie ends the film blind and paraplegic, having absorbed the physical cost of protecting others. That is a traditional heroism arc played straight, and it is the one thing the film does not completely botch.

Adam Scott's Ben Parker provides the film's only warmth. His scenes with Johnson are the one relationship in the film that feels like actual human interaction. His character's kindness, reliability, and quiet decency are traditionally masculine virtues played without irony.

But these elements cannot rescue the film from its fundamental problems: a script that insults the audience's intelligence, a lead performance that registers as checked out, a villain whose audio does not sync with his mouth, pacing that lurches between boring and baffling, and CGI that looks like it was rendered on a deadline three weeks too tight.

Madame Web is not a culture-war flashpoint. It is not offensive enough to provoke outrage or good enough to earn defense. It is simply bad. Impressively, consistently, almost fascinatingly bad. The kind of bad where you stop being angry and start being curious about how so many professionals at a major studio looked at this film and said yes, this is ready for theaters. The answer, as usual with Sony's Spider-Man Universe, is that the studio's desperation to exploit its Marvel IP license overrode every creative instinct that might have saved the project.

The film's lasting cultural contribution is becoming a punchline. The memes are funnier than the movie. Dakota Johnson's dead-eyed press tour became more entertaining than her performance. Tahar Rahim's dubbed dialogue became more discussed than his character's motivation. And the line from the trailer, "He was in the Amazon with my mom when she was researching spiders right before she died," became shorthand for clumsy exposition in an era that was already drowning in it.

Sony killed the Spider-Man Universe shortly after this film's release. Good.
summary.adultInsight: Conservative adults will not find much to be offended by here, because there is not much of anything here. The woke content is mild: a deportation backstory, a girls-in-STEM shirt, a scene mocking traditional femininity at a baby shower. None of it is sustained or coherent enough to constitute an ideological agenda. The bigger problem for conservative audiences is simply that the film is unwatchable. It is poorly written, poorly acted (with the exception of Adam Scott), poorly paced, and poorly edited. The maternal sacrifice theme at the core is genuinely traditional, and the final image of Cassie as a blind, paraplegic mentor who gave her body to save others has real weight. But getting to that moment requires enduring two hours of the worst dialogue, the most nonsensical plotting, and the most disengaged lead performance of any superhero film in recent memory. Your time is better spent elsewhere.
summary.parentalGuidance: Rated PG-13 for violence and action. Recommended for viewers 10 and older. The violence is standard superhero fare: fights, chases, and a villain with spider-like abilities who kills people with a neurotoxin. The opening scene features a pregnant woman being shot and killed, which is the film's most intense moment. Three teenage girls are repeatedly stalked and hunted by an adult man, which may unsettle younger viewers at a conceptual level even though the execution is too inept to be genuinely frightening. No sexual content, nudity, strong language, or substance use. The biggest risk to younger viewers is not the content but the boredom. This is 116 minutes of their life they will not get back.

tropeAudit.name: All-Female Hero Ensemble
tropeAudit.description: The film's core ensemble is four women: one adult mentor and three teenage future heroes. The only significant male characters are the villain and Adam Scott's Ben Parker. The film was explicitly marketed as Sony's first female-centric Marvel film. The choice to center the Spider-Women characters, none of whom are A-list comic book properties, was clearly driven by a desire to build a female-led franchise. The all-female ensemble is not inherently woke, plenty of great films center women, but the corporate calculation behind it is transparent. The film does not earn its girl-power framing because the women are not given interesting things to do.

tropeAudit.name: Girl-Boss Empowerment Without Earning It
tropeAudit.description: Cassie's arc follows the modern girl-boss template: she starts as a reluctant loner with poor social skills, discovers she has powers, accepts her destiny, and defeats the male villain. But the film hands her every advantage without requiring her to earn anything. Her powers simply manifest. Her trip to Peru instantly delivers the answers she needs. The tribal chief puts her through a ritual that unlocks her abilities without meaningful cost or struggle. Her true potential is handed to her rather than developed through conflict, sacrifice, or growth. This is the girl-boss pattern at its laziest: empowerment as entitlement.

tropeAudit.name: Immigration as Sympathetic Backstory
tropeAudit.description: Anya Corazon's father was deported, leaving her to fend for herself as a teenager. This backstory is presented as straightforwardly sympathetic: immigration enforcement is the cause of a vulnerable child being abandoned. The film does not engage with the complexity of immigration policy. It simply uses deportation as a source of pathos. The detail is brief and does not drive the plot, but it represents a clear progressive editorial choice about which characters deserve sympathy and which government actions should be viewed as harmful.

tropeAudit.name: Traditional Femininity Mocked
tropeAudit.description: A baby shower scene contrasts Cassie's blunt, abrasive personality against a group of traditionally feminine women who are written as vapid and shallow. Cassie's discomfort at the shower is played for laughs, and the audience is positioned to sympathize with her rejection of traditional female socializing. The traditional women are not characters. They are props designed to make Cassie look edgy and different by comparison. This is a mild but recognizable pattern: traditional femininity as a punchline.

tropeAudit.name: Girls-in-STEM Signaling
tropeAudit.description: One of the teenage characters is depicted as gifted at math and wears a shirt with a slogan about girls doing math. The film briefly signals that female academic excellence, particularly in traditionally male-dominated fields, is something worth celebrating. It is a throwaway moment with no narrative impact, but it represents a recognizable progressive signaling choice in character design.

tropeAudit.name: Mystical Indigenous People as Plot Device
tropeAudit.description: The Peruvian Amazon tribe Las Aranas possesses mystical spider-based abilities and serves as the source of all the film's superpowers. In the 1973 prologue, they try to save Cassie's mother. In the present, their chief Santiago puts Cassie through a ritual that unlocks her clairvoyance. This is the noble savage trope repackaged: indigenous people exist in the narrative solely to provide spiritual wisdom and supernatural assistance to the Western protagonist. The tribe has no agency, no story of its own, and no perspective beyond serving as a mystical gas station for the white hero's journey.

tropeAudit.name: Maternal Sacrifice as Central Theme
tropeAudit.description: The film's emotional core is maternal sacrifice across two generations. Cassie's mother Constance died trying to save her daughter from myasthenia gravis. The spiders she sought in the Amazon were not for fame or research, but to heal her child. Cassie inherits this maternal imperative: she becomes the protector of three vulnerable girls, ultimately sacrificing her sight and mobility to save them. The film ends with Cassie blind and paralyzed but committed to mentoring the girls into their future. This is sacrificial motherhood played straight, and it is the one thematic throughline the film handles with genuine emotional weight.

tropeAudit.name: Self-Sacrifice for the Innocent
tropeAudit.description: Cassie's heroism is defined by what it costs her. She does not walk away from the final battle stronger, cooler, or more powerful. She walks away blind and paraplegic. The film treats this sacrifice as noble rather than tragic: Cassie's clairvoyance becomes clearer in her blindness, and she embraces her new role as a mentor. This is the classical heroism model where saving others requires absorbing real, permanent damage. The film earns this moment even though almost nothing before it works.

tropeAudit.name: Reliable Male Decency (Ben Parker)
tropeAudit.description: Adam Scott's Ben Parker is the film's moral anchor. He is a good man: kind, dependable, brave, and protective without being overbearing. He rushes his pregnant sister-in-law Mary to the hospital during the climax while Cassie fights the villain. He revives Cassie after her near-death experience. He represents quiet, traditionally masculine goodness, the kind of man who shows up, does the right thing, and does not ask for credit. The film does not undermine or ironize his decency. In a movie that fails at almost everything, Ben Parker works.
